Every call is a timed change to one {@cref CameraSetting}: a lerp moves it from one value to another, and {@cref Maintain} holds it where it is. When a change ends, the setting snaps back to what the game wants, so follow a lerp with {@cref Maintain} to keep its end value. Pass a `delay` to line up several changes back to back in one go, like the legs of a fly-through.

Your changes go in a group, {@cref DefaultContext} unless you pass your own id, and {@cref Clear} removes one group without touching the game's own camera effects. When two changes to the same setting overlap, the higher priority wins, and {@cref DefaultPriority} beats the game's.

The camera still bumps into walls, so pointing it at something behind geometry pulls it in close. And the world is still loaded around the hero, not the camera, so a camera sent far away can show missing scenery. Move the hero along with it if that matters.

doc.summary:
Per-recipient wire budget in bytes/s. Defaults to 16 KB/s.

This is the budget that matters: frames go out on the reliable net channel, which disconnects the client on overflow rather than throttling. Raise it only with real players on a real server, watching for choke and drops.

Frames per second this channel can actually deliver, derived from {@cref CaptionLengthSeconds} and the client's six-caption display pool. Read-only.

Pace recurring updates against this. Offering frames faster than the channel drains does not increase throughput — it just grows the queue and adds latency, because a frame is only as useful as the moment it arrives. Your achievable byte rate is roughly `MaxFramesPerSecond × bytes-per-update`; to go faster, send more per frame rather than more frames.

members.signature: public static float CaptionLengthSeconds { get; set; }

doc.summary:
How long each caption frame lives on the client, in seconds. Defaults to 0.2.

This governs throughput, not bandwidth. The client renders at most six captions at a time and silently discards any beyond that, so the channel tops out at `6 / CaptionLengthSeconds` frames per second — about 5/s at the game's default linger, which is why the transport felt slow regardless of rate or frame size. The send rate is clamped to stay inside this automatically.

Lower means more throughput but less time for the client to build its panel and for the mod to read it. Do not go near a frame time.

This is not a knob you set to change client behaviour — the addon owns that. It exists so {@cref MaxFramesPerSecond} tells the truth. If you ship an addon with a different `CC_LINGER`, set the same value here or the channel will pace itself against a pool that recycles slower than it thinks.

doc.summary:
Change one style property on a node already in the panel's tree, without rebuilding it.

`nodeId` is the node's `Id`, resolved client-side. Patches coalesce latest-wins per `(node, property)`, so calling this every frame is safe: offering updates faster than the channel drains costs nothing but intermediate values. {@cref BuildLayout} has no such coalescing — driving it per-frame grows an unbounded backlog and the panel falls progressively further behind.

For anything whose path is known in advance, prefer one patch plus a CSS transition over a stream of them:

```csharp
UI.Panel("hud").SetStyle(to, "bar", "transition-duration", "30s");
UI.Panel("hud").SetStyle(to, "bar", "width", "0%");
```

The client then interpolates at its own framerate, which is smoother than this channel could ever be and costs nothing after the first patch.

doc.summary: A box in the world that tells you when players walk into it and out of it, through {@cref Entered} and {@cref Left}. Use it for checkpoints, start and finish lines, reset areas, safe areas, or anything else you'd otherwise check by hand every frame.
doc.remarks:
Zones check each player's position every game tick. The position is at the hero's feet, so to catch a player standing in an area, start the box a little below the floor and go up to about head height. Dead players, and players who haven't picked a hero yet, count as outside every zone.

Because positions are only checked once a tick, a fast player (dashing, on a zipline) can cross a thin zone between two checks without ever being inside. Make zones that catch moving players, like finish lines, at least 100 units deep in the direction they're crossed.

A zone keeps working until you call {@cref Dispose} or your plugin unloads. To show it in the world, draw it with `CBeam.CreateBox(zone.Mins, zone.Maxs)`.
